801.event_title: Theo van Gogh refuses to treat his brother's requests as a debt
801.event: From about 1880 until 1890, Theo van Gogh, an art dealer in Paris, sent his brother Vincent regular remittances, estimated at around 17,500 francs in total, that made Vincent's career as a painter possible. Vincent often asked for more and wrote of the money as something he owed. In letters of 1888 and 1889 Theo replied that he knew nothing of any debt and that Vincent had repaid him several times over through his work and his brotherly affection.
801.explanation: Theo's support was one of the main reasons Vincent could keep painting through ten years with almost no sales, and Theo consistently treated Vincent's constant claims on him as a natural part of their bond rather than as impositions.
801.tie_back: The kural defines long-standing closeness as the bond that never belittles the claims an intimate makes on it, and Theo answered Vincent's repeated requests by denying there was any debt at all.
801._accuracy_note: A strong picture of a bond that never resented the liberties of intimacy, though it is between brothers rather than old friends.

802.event_title: Elgar's Enigma Variations portray his friends with affectionate humour
802.event: Between October 1898 and February 1899 Edward Elgar composed a set of orchestral variations in which each variation is a musical portrait of one of his circle, often built on a friend's quirks or on humorous incidents, such as an organist's bulldog falling into a river and paddling out. He dedicated the work to the friends pictured in it, and his publisher and close friend August Jaeger appeared as Nimrod. The work was first performed under Hans Richter on 19 June 1899 and became Elgar's breakthrough.
802.explanation: The Enigma Variations turned the teasing familiarity of a circle of friends into one of the best-loved works of English music, with the affectionate Nimrod variation now used at national commemorations.
802.tie_back: The kural says the freedoms friends take with one another are part of friendship itself and that the wise relish them, and Elgar's friends were immortalised precisely through the playful liberties he took with their foibles.
802._accuracy_note: Illustrates friendly liberty as part of friendship well, but the sources document Elgar's side more than his friends' delight in it.

803.event_title: Louis Howe writes and speaks for Franklin Roosevelt during his illness
803.event: After Franklin Roosevelt was paralysed by illness in 1921, his old friend and adviser Louis Howe kept Roosevelt before the public by meeting supporters, attending meetings on his behalf and writing editorials and magazine articles, some published under Roosevelt's own byline. Roosevelt kept Howe as his closest counsellor, valued his frank advice and, after winning the presidency, made him his personal secretary with a room in the White House. Howe continued to speak bluntly to Roosevelt until his death in 1936.
803.explanation: Howe's work in Roosevelt's name helped carry him from apparent political ruin to the governorship of New York and the presidency.
803.tie_back: The kural asks what use a long friendship is if one will not accept what the friend does by right of closeness as though one had done it oneself, and Roosevelt allowed Howe's words to go out under his own name.
803._accuracy_note: Close fit to owning a friend's acts as one's own, though the work was a deliberate political partnership as well as a friendship.

804.event_title: Emerson's friends rebuild his house and send him abroad after a fire
804.event: On 24 July 1872 a fire badly damaged Ralph Waldo Emerson's house in Concord, destroying the roof and much of the second floor. Without being asked, Emerson's friends raised money to restore the house; his Harvard classmate Francis Cabot Lowell personally delivered a gift of 5,000 dollars from himself and other friends, and Judge Ebenezer Hoar presented a further sum collected to pay for a journey to Europe and Egypt. Emerson accepted, travelled with his daughter Ellen, and returned on 27 May 1873 to find the house restored and the town waiting to welcome him.
804.explanation: The episode shows a community of old friends acting on its own initiative to rescue a dispirited friend, and Emerson's grateful acceptance of what they had arranged.
804.tie_back: The kural says the wise welcome what close friends do for them unasked, as if they had wanted it themselves, and Emerson accepted both the rebuilding and the journey his friends had planned without consulting him.
804._accuracy_note: Very close dramatisation: friends acted without being asked and the recipient welcomed it.

805.event_title: Carlyle forgives John Stuart Mill after the French Revolution manuscript is burned
805.event: Thomas Carlyle gave his friend John Stuart Mill the only complete manuscript of the first volume of his history of the French Revolution for comment. While it was in Mill's household it was burned by a maid who mistook it for waste paper and used it to light a fire. Mill, distressed, paid Carlyle compensation; Carlyle rewrote the volume, the book was published in 1837, and Mill was one of the first to praise it.
805.explanation: Carlyle's response turned a disaster that could have ended the friendship into one of the most famous examples of literary forbearance, and the rewritten book made his reputation.
805.tie_back: The kural asks us to put down a hurtful act by a friend to ignorance or to the closeness that made them careless, and Carlyle treated the loss caused by Mill's household as an accident rather than an offence.
805._accuracy_note: Strong fit: a painful harm arising from a friend's trusted care was put down to accident and the friendship survived.

806.event_title: Vice President Truman attends the funeral of Tom Pendergast
806.event: Tom Pendergast, the Kansas City political boss who had backed Harry Truman's early career, was convicted of income tax evasion in 1939 and died on 26 January 1945. Truman, Vice President of the United States for little more than a week, attended the funeral despite considerable public controversy. In a statement he said that Pendergast had always been his friend and that he had always been Pendergast's.
806.explanation: Truman accepted damage to his own reputation at the start of his national career rather than abandon an old friend who had fallen into disgrace.
806.tie_back: The kural says those who keep to the true bounds of friendship will not give up a long-standing bond even when it brings them loss, and Truman stood by Pendergast's memory at real political cost.
806._accuracy_note: Near dramatisation of keeping an old bond despite the loss it brings, though the friend's wrongdoing makes the loyalty debatable.

807.event_title: Joachim keeps playing Brahms and accepts the Double Concerto after their rift
807.event: During the breakdown of violinist Joseph Joachim's marriage, Johannes Brahms wrote a private letter of support to Amalie Joachim that was later read in the divorce proceedings, and Joachim broke off their long friendship. Joachim nevertheless kept performing Brahms's music, and in 1887 Brahms wrote the Double Concerto for violin and cello as a gesture of reconciliation. Joachim rehearsed it with Brahms at Baden-Baden, played it at the premiere in Cologne in October 1887, and received the manuscript inscribed to him for whom it was written.
807.explanation: A friendship of more than thirty years survived a deep personal injury, and the reconciliation produced one of the great works of the violin repertoire.
807.tie_back: The kural says those whose friendship has come down a long road of love do not stop loving even when friends do things that bring them ruin, and Joachim went on championing Brahms's music after Brahms's letter had harmed him in court.
807._accuracy_note: Strong illustration, though Joachim did break off personal contact for some years before the reconciliation.

808.event_title: Queen Victoria defends Abdul Karim against her household
808.event: Abdul Karim arrived from Agra in 1887 to serve Queen Victoria, became her munshi, or teacher, in 1889, taught her Urdu and was later named her Indian Secretary. His rise caused turmoil within the royal household and among government officials, who tried to separate them and accused him of having access to political papers. The Queen supported him in every case, insisted he did not read political papers, and provided for him until her death in 1901.
808.explanation: The episode shows a monarch refusing to let courtiers' complaints undermine a trusted friendship, in a court where many of the objections reflected prejudice.
808.tie_back: The kural praises the person so secure in an intimate friendship that they will not even listen to talk of the friend's faults, and Victoria refused to hear her household's charges against Abdul Karim.
808._accuracy_note: Good fit to refusing to hear of a friend's faults; the kural's further claim that the friend's actual error becomes a day of gain is not shown.

809.event_title: Lafayette's farewell tour and his visit to Washington's tomb
809.place: United States, including Mount Vernon, Virginia
809.event: At President James Monroe's invitation, the Marquis de Lafayette returned to the United States in August 1824 and over the next year visited all twenty-four states, greeted by parades and crowds, including an estimated two-thirds of New York City on his arrival. On 17 October 1824 he visited the tomb of his old friend and mentor George Washington at Mount Vernon, leaving it in tears, and he renewed friendships with Jefferson, Madison and other veterans of the Revolution. Congress granted him 200,000 dollars and land, and towns and squares across the country were named in his honour.
809.explanation: Nearly fifty years after the Revolution, Lafayette's unbroken loyalty to Washington and to his American comrades made him the most celebrated guest the young nation had ever received.
809.tie_back: The kural says the world loves those who never let go of friendships that have come down unbroken through the years, and a whole nation turned out to honour Lafayette's lifelong fidelity to Washington and his old companions.
809._accuracy_note: Strong on public love for an old, faithful friend, though the welcome honoured Lafayette's Revolutionary service as well as his loyalty.

810.event_title: Simon Buckner, Grant's old friend and former enemy, honours him at the end
810.place: New York and Mount McGregor, New York, United States; Fort Donelson, Tennessee
810.event: In 1854 Simon Bolivar Buckner, Ulysses Grant's friend from West Point and the Mexican War, vouched for the penniless Grant's hotel bill in New York. When Buckner surrendered Fort Donelson to Grant in 1862, Grant demanded unconditional surrender but, remembering his old friend's kindness, offered him money for his captivity. In July 1885 Buckner, a former Confederate general, made a personal visit to the dying Grant at Mount McGregor and served as one of his pallbearers in New York in August 1885 alongside Union generals Sherman and Sheridan.
810.explanation: Grant's refusal to let war erase an old friendship was answered by a former enemy who chose to honour him, and the funeral became a symbol of reconciliation after the Civil War.
810.tie_back: The kural says those who never fall away from goodwill toward old friends are loved even by those who were against them, and Buckner, a general of the opposing army, came to honour Grant at his deathbed and his funeral.
810._accuracy_note: Very close fit: loyalty to an old friend across a war won the love of a former enemy.
